content.chapter: Chapter 1: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
objectives: Say what Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is and who wrote it.
Say why Mahmud Kashgari wrote the book.
Name three things that are in the book.
Use the past simple with years (in 1072).
content.pedagogy: The chapter introduces the book and its author. A simple timeline (1072 → 1074 → 1077) helps learners hold the dates, and a list of what is in the book (words, poems, legends, a map) shows why it is a guide to Turkish culture.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The book teaches Turkish to Arabs; it does not teach Arabic to Turks.
Kashgari presented the book in Baghdad; the only copy is in Istanbul today.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in + year · past simple (started, finished, presented)
Look (Activity 1): In 1072, … started writing.
Practise (Activity 2): fill started, finished, presented.
Likely errors: *on 1072 · *he finish it.
Use (Activity 3): a book I know.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: dî-VÂ-nu lu-GÂ-ti’t-TÜRK, MAH-mud kash-GA-ri.
Numbers: 1072 = ten seventy-two; 132,334 = one hundred thirty-two thousand, three hundred thirty-four.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the oldest book in your home?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the book and who wrote it?
Second reading: make a timeline with 1072, 1074 and 1077.
Find four things that are in the book.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Timeline; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a book I know; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Kashgari write the book?
What can people learn from the book?
Why is the map in the book important?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Millet Library” and “The Map” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: oldest, author, Dictionary of Turkish Languages, though, legends, describes, guide.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline with the first year filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about the book with the years.

formativeAssessment: Uses the past simple with years.
expectedResponses: Mahmud Kashgari wrote Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk in the 11th century. He wrote it to teach Turkish to Arabs. He started it in 1072 and finished it in 1074.
content.transferTask: Write about a book you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see why the book is a guide to Turkish culture?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “in” and a year about the book.

objectives: Say where and when Mahmud Kashgari was born and died.
Say what Kashgar is.
Retell how Kashgari describes himself.
Use was born in and adverbs with -ly.
content.pedagogy: A short chapter about the author’s life. His own words about himself give a model for a simple self-description, which learners write about themselves.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Kashgari was born in Barsgan, not in Kashgar; he died in Kashgar.
“Perfectly” is how he speaks; it is not a name of a language.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was born in + place / year · adverbs with -ly · great at + -ing
Look (Activity 1): was born in Barsgan in 1008.
Practise (Activity 2): choose perfectly, clearly and at.
Likely errors: *I born in · *great in throwing.
Use (Activity 3): this is me.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: BARS-gan, KASH-gar, kyr-gyz-STAN, ka-ra-KHA-nid.
Stress: PER-fect-ly, CLEAR-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where were you born? Where were your grandparents born?”
duringReading: First reading: Where was Kashgari born?
Second reading: make a card: born / died / family.
Find three things he says about himself.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Life card; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: this is me; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Where is Kashgar?
What does Kashgari say about his family?
What is he great at?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Kashgar” and “A Noble Family” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: Kashgar, East Turkestan (Doğu Türkistan), perfectly, throwing spears.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the life card with the headings born, died and family.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about yourself, like Kashgari.

formativeAssessment: Says where he was born and died.
expectedResponses: Mahmud Kashgari was born in Barsgan in 1008 and died in Kashgar in 1105. He came from a noble Karakhanid family. He spoke Turkish perfectly.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the author’s words as a model?

exitTicket: Write one sentence: “I was born in … in …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says where he was born and died.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: In Praise of the Turks and Their Language
objectives: Say what Kashgari writes about the Turks.
Explain why Kashgari traveled from tribe to tribe.
Explain why he wanted to praise Turkish.
Use to + verb for a purpose.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains the author’s purpose: he loved his native language and wanted to show it was as great as Arabic. A cause → purpose chart (Arabic in schools → praise Turkish → write the book) makes the reasons clear.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Arabic was the main language in Karakhanid schools; Kashgari wrote the book to praise Turkish.
He traveled for ten to fifteen years before he reached Baghdad, not after.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb (purpose) · from … to …
Look (Activity 1): began his journey … to visit every Turkic land.
Practise (Activity 2): choose to visit, to prove and to.
Likely errors: *for visit · *for to prove.
Use (Activity 3): why I learn.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: JOUR-ney, VAL-u-a-ble, DI-a-lects, ha-DITH.
Linking: “tribe to tribe” /traɪb tə traɪb/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know any Turkish dialects? Where do people speak them?”
duringReading: First reading: What does Kashgari say about the Turks?
Second reading: complete the chart: Arabic in schools → praise Turkish → book.
Find how long he traveled.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: why I learn; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What qualities of the Turks does Kashgari name?
What did he do on his journey?
Why did he want to praise Turkish?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Long Journey” and “Karakhanid Schools” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: qualities.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the first box filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about Kashgari’s journey with to + verb.

formativeAssessment: Names two qualities of the Turks.
Uses to + verb for a purpose.
expectedResponses: In Karakhanid schools, Arabic was the main language. Kashgari wanted to praise Turkish, so he traveled to every Turkic land and wrote his book to prove that Turkish was just as great as Arabic.
content.transferTask: Write about why you learn things.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “to + verb” about Kashgari.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the list of qualities.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Story of the Calendar
objectives: Retell the story of the Twelve-Animal calendar in order.
Explain why the khan wanted a calendar.
Say what a kurultay was.
Use let’s, if and so in a short story.
content.pedagogy: A legend with a clear problem and solution: people could not agree on a date, so the khan made a calendar. Learners see that a calendar is a shared record. The legend is read as Kashgari tells it.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of irregular verbs (went, told, could).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The khan did not choose the animals; the animals that crossed the river gave the years their names.
A kurultay was a national meeting, not a battle.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: let’s + verb · if + present, will · so · because · could + base verb
Look (Activity 1): let’s make a calendar.
Practise (Activity 2): fill so, cross and because.
Likely errors: *let’s to make · *could crossed.
Use (Activity 3): let’s do it together.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: KHAN, ku-rul-TAY, I-li VAL-ley.
Stress: CAL-en-dar, dis-a-GREED, SAFE-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do you remember important dates?”
duringReading: First reading: Why did the khan want a calendar?
Second reading: put four events in order.
Find which animal crossed first.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Story order; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: let’s do it together; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the calendar help the Turks keep track of?
Why did the khan call a kurultay?
Why did the calendar start with the rat?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Kurultay” and “The River” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: since ancient, keep track, disagreed, Kurultay, wild animals, Ili Valley, cross, safely, Rat.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four events on cards to order.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Act out the kurultay and the hunt in two short scenes.

formativeAssessment: Explains why the khan wanted a calendar.
expectedResponses: The people disagreed about the date of a battle, so the khan called a kurultay. He wanted a calendar for everyone. Twelve animals crossed a river, and the years got their names from them.
content.transferTask: Make a plan for your class with let’s.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners understand why a shared calendar was useful?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “let’s” and one with “because”.

objectives: Name the twelve animals of the calendar in English.
Say the order of the years with ordinal numbers.
Match old Turkic names with English names.
content.pedagogy: A list chapter: short, clear and good for vocabulary. Learners meet old Turkic words next to English ones, so the chapter also shows how a dictionary works. Keep the old names as they are in the book.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Nag means ‘Crocodile’ in this list; learners may expect a dragon from other calendars. Keep the book’s meaning.
Ordinal numbers end in -th after third: fourth, fifth … twelfth.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: ordinal numbers (first, second, third … twelfth) · means
Look (Activity 1): the third year.
Practise (Activity 2): choose first, second and twelfth.
Likely errors: *the one year · *the twelveth year.
Use (Activity 3): animals in my world.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Ordinals: first /fɜːrst/, second /ˈsekənd/, third /θɜːrd/, twelfth /twelfθ/.
Stress: CROC-o-dile, ROOST-er, LEOP-ard.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which animals can you name in English?”
duringReading: First reading: How many animals are there?
Second reading: circle the animals you know.
Find the old name for each bold animal.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Circle and say; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: animals in my world; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which animal is first? Which is last?
Which old names are like modern Turkish words?
Which animal is new for you?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Year of the Rat” and “Year of the Pig” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: Ox, Crocodile, Rooster.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give picture cards of the twelve animals.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the twelve animals in order with ordinal numbers.

expectedResponses: The Year of the Rat is the first year. The Year of the Ox is the second year. The Year of the Pig is the twelfth year.
content.transferTask: Talk about three animals from the list.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice how the list works like a dictionary?

exitTicket: Write one sentence: “The Year of the … is the … year.”

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the numbers in the list.

objectives: Explain the meanings of some years in the old beliefs.
Describe how the calendar counts time (cycle, months, hours).
Say what Nowruz is and when it starts.
Use because, but and so.
content.pedagogy: The chapter reports old beliefs about the years and facts about how the calendar counts time. Keep the line between “people believe” and facts clear: the beliefs belong to the old Turkic calendar as Kashgari describes it.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The beliefs about the years are old beliefs that the book reports; they are not rules for today.
One cycle lasts 12 years, not 12 months.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because · but · so · will (belief about the future)
Look (Activity 1): … because the ox is an animal that likes to fight.
Practise (Activity 2): choose but, because and So.
Likely errors: *because of the ox likes · *so because.
Use (Activity 3): a special day.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: CY-cle, MID-night, cel-e-BRA-ted.
Names: now-RUZ, BAL-kans.
beforeReading: Ask: “When does the new year start in your calendar?”
duringReading: First reading: What does each year mean?
Second reading: make a chart: year / meaning / reason.
Find when the old Turkish calendar started.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a special day; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why do people link the Year of the Ox with wars?
How long does one part of a day last?
Where did Turks celebrate Nowruz?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Year of the Ox” and “Nowruz” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: horns, trouble, lasts, celebrated, Nowruz (Nevruz).

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the Year of the Ox filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about the calendar with because and so.

formativeAssessment: Explains one year’s meaning with a reason.
Says how long a cycle lasts.
expectedResponses: In the old beliefs, the Year of the Ox brings more wars because the ox likes to fight. One cycle lasts 12 years. The new year started on March 21st, and Turks called it Nowruz.
content.transferTask: Write about a special day in your family.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate old beliefs from facts about counting time?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because” about the calendar.

rubricLevels.secure: Says how the calendar counts time.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The First World Map with Japan
objectives: Describe Kashgari’s world map: shape, colors and places.
Say what is in the middle of the map.
Say which places the map shows in the west, south and east.
Use directions: in the north / south / east / west.
content.pedagogy: The chapter describes a map, so learners can draw while they read. A blank circle on the board, filled step by step with the places in the chapter, makes the text visual. The book’s view of the map (Turkestan in the middle) is read as Kashgari describes it.
anticipatedMisconceptions: On the map, China is called ‘the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc’; ‘Jabarqa’ is the name for Japan.
The second map with Japan was made four hundred years after this book, not before.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in the north / south / east / west · in the middle · as far west as
Look (Activity 1): In the east, it shows China and Japan.
Practise (Activity 2): fill west, south and east.
Likely errors: *in east · *on the middle.
Use (Activity 3): a map of my town.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ba-la-sa-GUN, ja-BAR-qa, I-dil.
Stress: COL-or-ful, de-SIGN.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can you see on a map?”
duringReading: First reading: What is in the middle of the map?
Second reading: draw the map with the colors and places.
Find the old names of Japan and China.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–20 Draw the map; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–33 Language Focus 1–2; 33–38 Use: a map of my town; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Turkestan in the middle of the map?
Why was Balasagun an important city?
Why is this map important today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Balasagun” and “Japan on the Map” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: Silk Road, Yecüc and Mecüc.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a circle with the colors already marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about the map with directions.

formativeAssessment: Says what is in the middle.
expectedResponses: Kashgari’s map is round and colorful. Turkestan is in the middle. In the east, it shows China and Japan. It is the first world map to show Japan.
content.transferTask: Draw and describe a map of your town.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the text to build the map?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “in the east” or “in the west” about the map.

rubricLevels.secure: Says what is in the middle.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: A Treasure of the Turkish Language
objectives: Say why Kashgari’s book is a treasure of the Turkish language.
Say what UNESCO did in 2024.
Name countries that worked together for the celebration.
Use superlatives (the oldest, the biggest).
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter links the 11th-century book with today: a UNESCO celebration and many Turkic countries working together. It invites learners to see the book as a living treasure.
anticipatedMisconceptions: UNESCO included the book in its program at Turkey’s suggestion; the book was not written in 2024.
The superlative needs “the”: the biggest, the oldest.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: superlatives (the oldest, the biggest) · very + adjective
Look (Activity 1): the biggest treasure.
Practise (Activity 2): choose oldest, biggest and important.
Likely errors: *the most big · *biggest treasure (without the).
Use (Activity 3): a treasure of my culture.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: yu-NES-co, a-zer-bai-JAN, ka-zakh-STAN, uz-BEK-i-stan.
Stress: TREA-sure, sug-GES-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is a treasure? Can a book be a treasure?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is the book a treasure?
Second reading: list the countries.
Find the year of the UNESCO program.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–15 Country list; 15–19 Quick Challenge; 19–30 Language Focus 1–2; 30–37 Use: a treasure of my culture; 37–40 Exit ticket. (Poster in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: Why is the book a treasure?
Why did many countries work together on it?
What secrets can new students learn from it?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “UNESCO” and “A Treasure” when the picture is in place.
The group task “Our Twelve-Animal Calendar Poster” closes the book.
Word Notes: suggestion.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a list of the countries with the first letter of each.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about the book with superlatives.

formativeAssessment: Says why the book is a treasure.
expectedResponses: Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the biggest treasure of the Turkish language. At Turkey’s suggestion, UNESCO included it in its 2024 program, and many Turkic countries worked together on it.
content.transferTask: Talk about a treasure of your culture.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link the old book with today?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “the oldest” or “the biggest” about the book.

rubricLevels.secure: Says why the book is a treasure.

metadata.title: Mahmud Kashgari A2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Mahmud Kashgari and His Work Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk (Kaşgarlı Mahmud)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Young learners and adults who can read short, simple texts about people, places and traditions, and who can write short connected sentences.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Mahmud Kashgari and his dictionary Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk: the author’s life and purpose, the Twelve-Animal calendar, Nowruz and the first world map to show Japan, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned in small steps: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence, then PRACTISE it in controlled, meaningful tasks, and finally USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 8 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture or a word from daily life.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a description, a list, a timeline or a story in order.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (look → practise → use), then a short production about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Text-based and in small steps. Start from the story sentence, ask a simple meaning question (What does this word show?), let learners answer, then confirm the rule and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: in + year · past simple (started, finished, presented)
Ch2: was born in + place / year · adverbs with -ly · great at + -ing
Ch4: let’s + verb · if + present, will · so · because · could + base verb
Ch5: ordinal numbers (first, second, third … twelfth) · means
Ch6: because · but · so · will (belief about the future)
Ch7: in the north / south / east / west · in the middle · as far west as
Ch8: superlatives (the oldest, the biggest) · very + adjective

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people, places and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find key information, follow a timeline or a list and understand simple reasons.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe people, places and special days in short connected sentences.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write short connected sentences with and, but, so and because.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for older people and for one’s language.
D3 Diligence — Long, patient work to reach a goal.
D16 Responsibility — Thinking about the people who come after us.
D6 Honesty — Being honest as a quality of good people.
languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (3 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts and timelines given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
The beliefs about the meaning of each year belong to the old Turkic calendar as Kashgari describes it; present them as old beliefs, not as rules or predictions for today.
The hadith and the sentences about Allah in Chapters 3 and 7 belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment.
Bracketed Turkish words and old Turkic animal names belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Mahmud Kashgari’s dictionary links the 11th-century Turkic world with questions every community faces today: how to keep a language alive, how to record shared time and how to learn about other nations.

themes.title: Keeping a language alive:
themes.description: Kashgari collected words, proverbs and poems from many tribes (Chapters 1 and 3). Discuss how people protect languages today.

themes.title: Shared time:
themes.description: The khan wanted a calendar so that people would agree on dates (Chapter 4). Compare different calendars and new year days, such as Nowruz (Chapter 6).

themes.title: Learning about the world:
themes.description: Kashgari’s map shows the nations the Turks met, from Russia to Japan (Chapter 7). Discuss what maps teach us about other people.

actions: Ask an older family member for an old word and write it down with its meaning.
Make a short poster about Nowruz and how people celebrate it.
Find Kashgar, Balasagun and Baghdad on a modern map.

exitTicket: One thing I learned about Mahmud Kashgari today is …
One new word from today’s chapter is …
One good action I can do this week is …

miniProject.title: Our Twelve-Animal Calendar Poster
miniProject.desc: In groups, draw a big circle with twelve parts. Write the twelve animals in order with their old Turkic names, add one sentence from the book and present why Kashgari’s book is a treasure.

reflectivePrompt.title: Words in My Family
reflectivePrompt.desc: Kashgari collected words from every Turkic tribe (Chapter 3). Write four to five sentences about an old word that someone in your family uses. What does it mean?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: Kashgari writes that the Turks are respectful to older people, and he wanted to praise his native language (Chapter 3).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Kashgari traveled from tribe to tribe for about ten to fifteen years and revised his book many times (Chapters 1 and 3).

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: The khan wanted a calendar so that the people after him would not be wrong about dates (Chapter 4).

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty: Kashgari names honesty among the great qualities of the Turks (Chapter 3).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.
practice: Chapter 4 (The Story of the Calendar): Put the events of the legend in order.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like “and”, “but” and “because”.
practice: Chapter 6 (What Each Year Means): Write three sentences about a special day in your family.
Language Review, “Use: Words in My Family”: Write four to five sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can give a simple description or presentation of people, living or working conditions, daily routines, likes/dislikes, etc. as a short series of simple phrases and sentences linked into a list.
practice: Chapter 2 (Who Was Mahmud Kashgari?): Describe yourself in three sentences.
Chapter 8 (A Treasure of the Turkish Language): Present the class calendar poster.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
objectives: I can say what Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is.
I can say why Mahmud Kashgari wrote it.
I can use started, finished and presented with years.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “In 1072, … started writing”: in + year. Then fill started, finished and presented.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: MAH-mud kash-GA-ri. Say: dî-VÂ-nu lu-GÂ-ti’t-TÜRK.
content.lessonPlan: What is the oldest book in your home? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find who wrote the book. Make a timeline: 1072, 1074, 1077.
discussionPoints: Kashgari wanted to show that Turkish is a rich language. What do you like about your language?

metadata.title: Mahmud Kashgari A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who read about Mahmud Kashgari alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of Mahmud Kashgari.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Understand who Mahmud Kashgari was and why he wrote Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk.
Retell the story of the Twelve-Animal calendar and describe Kashgari’s world map.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One thing about Mahmud Kashgari or his book that I liked:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 3 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, diligence, responsibility and honesty. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Kashgari writes that the Turks are respectful to older people, and he wanted to praise his native language (Chapter 3).
Diligence: Diligence: Kashgari traveled from tribe to tribe for about ten to fifteen years and revised his book many times (Chapters 1 and 3).
Responsibility: Responsibility: The khan wanted a calendar so that the people after him would not be wrong about dates (Chapter 4).
Honesty: Honesty: Kashgari names honesty among the great qualities of the Turks (Chapter 3).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of the Twelve-Animal calendar to someone at home in four sentences, in your home language or in English.
